opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to acknowledge is that we really don't know which approaches will work, and we don't have much time. So the rational response to that kind of uncertainty is not to bet everything on one research agenda. It's to diversify, the way you would with any high-stakes investment where you can't predict the outcome.

Right now, a lot of the safety effort is concentrated on making the current paradigm a bit safer after the fact: fine-tuning with human feedback, red-teaming, evaluations. These are useful, and we should keep doing them, but they're a bit like patching a system whose internals we don't understand. We see examples of models that deceive, that try to preserve themselves, that game their objectives. They come from how we train these systems: imitating humans and then optimizing for reward. Those methods naturally give rise to agency and goals we didn't intend, and we don't yet have reliable ways to detect or prevent that.

So part of my answer is that we should also invest seriously in approaches that are safe by design, not just safe by testing. One direction I've been pushing is what I call "Scientist AI": systems that aren't agents, that don't have goals of their own, but are trained to explain the world and give calibrated probabilities, honest answers about what is true, including their own uncertainty. A system like that could be very useful for science, and it could also serve as a guardrail: you could ask it, "What's the probability that this action proposed by some agentic AI causes serious harm?" and reject the action if that probability is too high. The key idea is to separate understanding from wanting, intelligence from agency.

And I'd add a couple of things. One is that uncertainty should push us toward precaution, not complacency. If there's even a moderate probability that we lose control over systems smarter than us, that's an unacceptable risk, and we should act as though it's real. Second, technical work alone isn't enough. Even if we find a good technical solution, we need governance and coordination so that it's actually adopted, and so that nobody cuts corners in a race. Companies and countries competing to be first is exactly the condition under which safety gets sacrificed.

So: a portfolio of research bets, more emphasis on designs that are safe from the ground up, humility about what we know, and policy that buys us the time to get it right.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a moderate probability of losing control is unacceptable, but it does not state a 1% chance or identify that threshold as Bengio’s view.

r002.rationale: It advocates diversifying research bets and pursuing multiple safety approaches rather than relying on one agenda.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not say that a promising technical safety path could be realized in less than a decade.

r004.rationale: The candidate does not state that a promising safety path can reuse tools underlying today’s most advanced AI systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the uncertainty itself should shape the strategy. If we were confident that, say, reinforcement learning from human feedback plus interpretability would get us to safe superhuman systems, then we could put most of our eggs in that basket. But we are not confident, and I think honestly anyone who is confident is not looking carefully at the evidence. So the rational response to deep uncertainty is a portfolio, and a portfolio that is deliberately diverse, not just many variations on the same idea.

Let me say what I mean by diverse. Most of the current effort in the labs is focused on making agents that behave well, which is natural because that is what the products are. You train the system, you try to shape its goals through feedback, you try to look inside with interpretability tools, you red-team it. All of that is valuable and I do not want to dismiss it. But there is a structural problem, which is that we are trying to control the goals of a system whose goals we cannot really read, and whose capabilities may eventually exceed our ability to evaluate its behavior. So the approaches that depend on us catching bad behavior after the fact are exactly the ones most likely to fail when it matters most, when the system is smarter than the evaluators.

That is why I have been pushing in a different direction, which is to ask whether we can build systems that are not agents at all, or at least whose core is not an agent. What I have called the scientist AI idea is that you build a system whose job is to understand the world, to produce explanations and predictions with calibrated uncertainty, but which does not have goals of its own in the sense of trying to change the world to satisfy some objective. A system like that can still be enormously useful, for science, for medicine, and it can also serve as a guardrail, because you can ask it what is the probability that this action by some other agent leads to harm, and refuse the action if that probability is too high. The point is that this is a bet on a different part of the design space, and if the mainstream approaches turn out to be fundamentally limited, we want to have something else ready.

The second thing I would say is that we need to treat this more like a scientific problem and less like an engineering competition. In science, when you are uncertain, you design experiments to reduce the uncertainty, you try to falsify your own hypotheses, you build theory. Right now there is a lot of empirical work and very little theory about what safety guarantees could even look like. I would like to see much more effort on the question of what would count as evidence that a system is safe, and on formal or semi-formal methods where you can bound the probability of catastrophic outcomes rather than just saying we tested it a lot and nothing went wrong. Testing can show the presence of problems, it cannot show their absence, and with these systems the absence is what we care about.

Third, and this is where I think the technical and the governance questions cannot be separated, we should invest in the kinds of safety work that remain useful even if the hard problem of alignment is not solved. Things like evaluations for dangerous capabilities, hardware-level controls, the ability to verify what a system is being used for, mechanisms for an off switch that actually works. These are not solutions, but they buy time, and time is the most valuable resource when you are uncertain, because it lets the science catch up.

And finally, I think we should be honest about the possibility that none of this is enough and that the correct answer at some point might be to slow down. That is not a technical answer, but it is a consequence of taking the uncertainty seriously. If you are driving in the fog, you can improve your headlights, you can improve your brakes, and you should do all of that, but you also drive slower. I do not think we should wait for a proof that something is dangerous before we act. The burden should be on showing that it is safe, and right now nobody can show that. So the research agenda, in my mind, is partly about building the tools, partly about building the understanding, and partly about making sure that if the tools and the understanding arrive too late, we have not already committed to something irreversible.

r001.rationale: The response says the burden should be on showing AI is safe and that development may need to slow down, but it does not state that even a 1% chance of catastrophe is unacceptable.

r002.rationale: It explicitly recommends a deliberately diverse portfolio of safety approaches, including non-agent scientist AI, scientific research, and measures such as evaluations and hardware controls.

r003.rationale: The response gives no claim about how long a promising safety path might take or whether it could be realized within a decade.

r004.rationale: The response does not state that a promising path can reuse tools underlying today’s most advanced AI systems.

astra-6.text:
I think we should pursue a portfolio of approaches. We don’t know which ones will work, and we should be careful not to confuse progress on a benchmark with evidence that a system will remain safe as it becomes more capable.

Some of the work should address the systems we have today: understanding how they make decisions, evaluating dangerous capabilities, and developing better ways to detect when our safeguards fail. But we also need research that questions the assumptions behind those systems. Can we build useful AI without giving it open-ended goals or incentives to resist human intervention? Can we design systems for which stronger safety guarantees are possible?

These directions are complementary. The more fundamental research may take longer, but that is a reason to start it now. And the nearer-term work can provide evidence about where our assumptions are wrong.

The crucial point is that uncertainty about whether safety research will succeed cannot itself justify proceeding as though it has succeeded. We should continue the research while making deployment decisions depend on the strength of the evidence we actually have.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention a 1% chance of catastrophe or say that such a risk is unacceptable to Bengio.

r002.rationale: It explicitly recommends a portfolio of complementary safety approaches, including work on current systems and more fundamental research.

r003.rationale: It says fundamental research may take longer and should start now, but does not state that a promising path need not take a decade.

r004.rationale: It asks whether useful AI can be built without open-ended goals, but does not say that a promising safety path can reuse tools underlying today’s most advanced AI systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should be humble about how much we know. We don’t currently have a method that gives us strong assurance that a very capable AI system will behave safely in situations we haven’t anticipated. But that uncertainty is a reason to invest in research, and to explore several approaches in parallel.

One direction is to improve our ability to understand and evaluate the systems we’re building. Another is to develop methods that could provide stronger safety guarantees, while being explicit about the assumptions those guarantees depend on. We should also investigate designs that avoid some of the difficulties of autonomous agents—for example, systems whose role is to help us understand the world without themselves pursuing goals in it.

The important thing is to avoid confusing progress on a benchmark with having solved the problem. We need to actively look for ways our methods could fail, and update our confidence when we find them. And research has to be connected to decisions about deployment: if we cannot establish sufficient safety, we need the ability to slow down. Otherwise, uncertainty becomes something we acknowledge in papers but ignore in practice.
